title: Power — how fast energy gets transferred
examTip: Power is measured in watts (W). 1 W = 1 J/s. Don't mix up power (the rate of energy transfer) with energy (the total amount transferred).
introTips: Power is about how fast energy is transferred. It is not about how much energy in total.
A weightlifter who raises a barbell slowly does the same work as one who raises it quickly. But the faster one has more power.
Watts and joules per second are the same thing: 1 W = 1 J/s.
intro: A crane that lifts a car in 5 seconds is more powerful than one that takes 20 seconds. Yet both do exactly the same job. Power tells you how quickly energy is transferred. It is why a sports car feels different to a city car. That is true even if both reach the same speed in the end. It is also why a 2 kW kettle boils water faster than a 1 kW one. And it is why power stations are rated in megawatts. Power lets you compare machines, work out costs and solve real exam questions.

keyPoints.heading: What power means
keyPoints.content: Power is the rate of energy transfer. It is how much energy is transferred per second. The equation is: P = E/t (power = energy ÷ time). The unit of power is the watt (W). 1 W = 1 joule per second. You can also write it as P = W/t, where W is work done (in joules). A powerful machine doesn't always transfer more energy overall. It transfers the same energy in a shorter time. Example: a crane lifting a car does the same work whether it takes 5 seconds or 20 seconds. It transfers the same energy. But the crane that does it in 5 seconds has four times the power. P = E/t, so for the same E, halving t doubles P.

keyPoints.memTip: P = E/t. Power is 'energy per second'.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Power and energy are easy to mix up. A 2 kW kettle and a 1 kW kettle transfer the same energy to boil the water. But the 2 kW one does it twice as fast.

keyPoints.heading: Calculating power
keyPoints.content: The main equation is P = E/t. Rearrangements: E = Pt (energy = power × time) and t = E/P (time = energy ÷ power). Worked example 1: a light bulb transfers 1800 J in 3 minutes (= 180 s) → P = 1800 ÷ 180 = 10 W. Worked example 2: a runner does 12,000 J of work in 60 s → P = 12,000 ÷ 60 = 200 W. Worked example 3: how long does a 2 kW (2000 W) heater take to transfer 36,000 J? t = E/P = 36,000 ÷ 2000 = 18 s. Unit conversions you must know: 1 kW = 1000 W. 1 MW = 1,000,000 W. Always convert to standard units (W and s) before calculating.

keyPoints.memTip: Triangle trick: put P at the top, and E and t at the bottom. Cover what you want to find: P = E/t, E = Pt, t = E/P.
keyPoints.tutor_note: It is easy to forget to convert minutes to seconds, or kW to W. Make a unit check a habit.

keyPoints.heading: Power in everyday contexts
keyPoints.content: Putting real numbers on power helps you make sense of the world. - Human body at rest: ~80 W, just keeping warm and breathing. - Walking: ~300 W. - Cycling: ~100–400 W, depending on speed. - Running: ~500–800 W. Top sprinters may briefly reach 2000 W. - Hairdryer: ~2000 W (2 kW). - Electric kettle: ~2000–3000 W. - Electric car motor: 100–300 kW. - Large power station: ~1–2 GW (gigawatts = 1,000,000,000 W). A professional Tour de France cyclist can keep up about 400 W for an hour. That is impressive, but far less than even a small electric motor. This is exactly why the Industrial Revolution changed so much. Steam engines could replace dozens of human workers by giving out many kilowatts non-stop.

keyPoints.heading: Work done and power — force × velocity
keyPoints.content: Work done (W) = force (F) × distance (d), when the force and movement are in the same direction. Units: joules (J). When a force acts through a distance, energy is transferred. We say 'work is done'. Power can also be written as: P = Fv (power = force × velocity). This comes from P = W/t = Fd/t = F × (d/t) = Fv. Units: N × m/s = W. Worked example: a car engine gives a driving force of 3000 N. It moves at a constant velocity of 20 m/s → P = 3000 × 20 = 60,000 W = 60 kW. This form is very useful when you are given a force and a speed, not energy and time. At constant velocity, the driving force equals the total resistive forces (drag + friction). So P = Fv gives you the engine power needed.

1.question: A runner does 18,000 J of work in 90 seconds. What is their power output?
1.correctFeedback: Correct! P = E/t = 18,000 ÷ 90 = 200 W. That is a sensible value for a runner.
1.wrongFeedback: Use P = E/t. Substitute: P = 18,000 J ÷ 90 s = 200 W. Remember to divide energy by time in seconds.

3.question: A car engine produces a driving force of 4000 N at a speed of 25 m/s. What is the engine's power output?
3.correctFeedback: Correct! P = Fv = 4000 × 25 = 100,000 W = 100 kW. That is a realistic value for a car engine.
3.wrongFeedback: Use P = Fv (power = force × velocity). P = 4000 N × 25 m/s = 100,000 W = 100 kW. Don't add force and velocity. Multiply them.

commonMistakes: Mixing up power (rate of energy transfer, W) with energy (total amount transferred, J). They are different quantities with different units.
Forgetting to convert minutes to seconds, or kW to W, before calculating. Always work in SI units (W and s).
Adding force and velocity instead of multiplying in P = Fv. Always multiply: P = F × v.
Thinking a more powerful device always transfers more energy. It transfers energy faster, not always more in total.
Leaving the unit off the answer. Power must be in W (or kW or MW, with conversion), not J or N.
examTips: P = E/t. If you see 'how fast' or 'rate of energy transfer', think power. If you see 'how much total energy', think E = Pt.
Convert units before calculating: kW → W (×1000), minutes → seconds (×60). Write the conversion step out clearly.
For P = Fv questions, check the units: newtons × metres per second = watts. This shows the formula is right.
If a question gives you efficiency and power together, find the useful output power. It equals efficiency × input power.
